title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what the page says, and what it does not

questions.prompt: Here is one sentence taken from a finished biography: "After his father lost the workshop, he left school at fifteen and joined a company of travelling players." Which set of notes was it written from?

options.text: father lost the workshop · left school at 15 · joined travelling players
father lost the workshop · left school at 15 · founded a company of players
father sold the workshop · left school at 15 · joined travelling players
father lost the workshop · joined a company of travelling players at 15

questions.explanation: Read the sentence backwards, fact by fact, and keep only the file that holds all of them and nothing else. Losing a workshop and selling one are two different events, and a family that sells has chosen while a family that loses has not. Joining a company and founding one are two different lives: the first man walks into something that already exists, the second builds it. And the age belongs to the leaving of school, not to the joining of the company — a small displacement, but the reader of the biography now believes something the file never said. This is the checking an examiner does: the notes are the evidence, and every word of the paragraph has to be traceable to them.

questions.prompt: The dictionary entry for "stage" ends, after all its senses, with a short list of fixed expressions. In which of these sentences must you read that final list to understand the line?

options.text: The actors were already waiting in the dark at the side of the wooden stage.
A wooden stage had been built at the far end of the covered market.
The company will stage three of the Bard's plays in the old quarry.
The festival's success set the stage for a second theatre in the town.

questions.explanation: Nothing was set out and no theatre stood on any raised floor: the success made a second theatre possible, and that meaning cannot be assembled from the words taken one by one. Expressions of this kind are filed at the end of an entry precisely because the senses above them will not produce them, and a reader who stops at the numbered senses will read the sentence four times without getting anywhere. The three other lines are made of the entry's ordinary material — the raised floor in two of them, the verb that puts a play in front of an audience in the third — and each of them can be understood by picking the right half and the right sense.

questions.prompt: A festival page prints one line for each show: "KEF — the Sundial Players in A Winter Night, directed by Nadia Ferchichi — the old fort — 2 to 16 August — tickets 8 dinars". A pupil fills his table: Play — A Winter Night · Troupe — the Sundial Players · Venue — Kef · Dates — 2 to 16 August. One cell does not hold what its column asks for. Which cell must he change?

options.text: the Play cell — the show is called The Sundial Players
the Dates cell — the show is given on 2 and on 16 August
the Venue cell — the show is put on in the old fort
the Troupe cell — the company is led by Nadia Ferchichi

questions.explanation: The line names a town and a building, and only one of the two is where an audience sits down. Kef tells a traveller which bus to take; the old fort tells him where the performance is, and that is what the column is for. The other three cells are already right. The title is the one printed after the name of the players, who are the people performing it and not the work itself. The woman named after the title directs the company but is not the company. And a dash between two dates opens the whole stretch between them, so reading it as two separate evenings would empty a fortnight of performances down to a pair.

questions.prompt: A newspaper article and a festival programme cover the same evening, but they are not written to do the same job. Which of these lines has been lifted from the programme itself?

options.text: The play will be given at the old fort every night from 2 to 16 August.
The Sundial Players open their season at the old fort on 2 August.
A Winter Night — the old fort, Kef — 2 to 16 August — 8 dinars
Tickets for the performances at the old fort cost eight dinars.

questions.explanation: All four lines carry the same evening; what separates them is whether anybody has bothered to make a sentence out of it. A programme entry keeps the fields apart with dashes and throws the verbs away, because it is a record to be looked up rather than a text to be read through. The three others are prose: each has a subject and a verb, and each takes one piece of the same information and builds a sentence round it. Recognising the difference is what lets you turn the record into your own sentences afterwards — and it is the same difference as the one between a box of notes and the biography written from it.

questions.prompt: A travel page carries this line above a festival programme: "By N. Selmi · Associated Press · Oct. 11, 2006". A pupil copies the programme's days and prices straight into the guide he is writing for next summer's visitors. What is wrong with what he has done?

options.text: the figures were printed for readers in another country
the figures belong to a season that ended years ago
the figures come from an agency and not from the festival
the figures are set out in an order English does not use

questions.explanation: The three lines of small print above an article say who wrote it, where it came from and when — and the third of those is the one a traveller cannot afford to skip. A festival keeps its name from one year to the next and changes almost everything else, so a page written more than a decade ago proves that the festival exists and proves nothing at all about next summer. The country the readers live in changes none of that, an agency is a perfectly reliable source for the year it was writing about, and the order of the words is a matter of style rather than of truth.

questions.prompt: A pupil's notes on a stage director read: "1946 born in Sousse · 1964 left for Tunis to study law · 1967 gave up law for the theatre · 1970 founded the Carthage Players · 1998 retired". Tick EVERY sentence below that says more than the notes allow.

options.text: In 1964 he left Sousse for Tunis, where he began to study law.
He gave up law in 1967 because his family had lost its money.
In 1970 he founded the Carthage Players, the finest troupe in the country.
He retired in 1998, after nearly thirty years at the head of his own company.
He was born in Sousse in 1946 and died in the same town fifty years later.

questions.explanation: Three of these five bring in something no note carries. A reason for abandoning the law appears nowhere, and neither does the state of anybody's fortune. A judgement is a claim like any other: the notes record that a troupe was founded, not that it was better than the rest. And a death has simply been made up, on a date the notes contradict, since the man is still working two years after it. The two remaining sentences invent nothing. One only rearranges a note into English. The other counts, and counting is allowed: the years 1970 and 1998 are both written down, and the twenty-eight between them are the pupil's own arithmetic rather than his imagination.
